subtitle: One-step inequalities: undo an addition, undo a multiplication, and turn the sign around when the divisor is negative

problems.desc: The graph must show an open circle at 7 with the line shaded to the left, covering every number below 7. A filled circle is wrong: 7 itself does not satisfy the inequality, because 7 plus 5 is 12 and 12 is not below 12.
The graph must show a filled circle at 7 with the line shaded to the right. The circle is filled because the sign allows equality, and 7 minus 3 is exactly 4.
The graph must show a filled circle at 5 with the line shaded to the left. Dividing by the positive 4 keeps the direction of the sign, so the shading goes the same way the original sign points.

The graph must show an open circle at negative 7 with the line shaded to the right. Watch that the circle sits to the left of zero: subtracting 9 from both sides gives a negative boundary even though both printed numbers are positive.
The graph must show an open circle at 6 with the line shaded to the right. The step here is multiplying both sides by the positive 3, which keeps the direction of the sign.

The graph must show a filled circle at negative 5 with the line shaded to the LEFT. Shading to the right is the classic error: dividing both sides by negative 2 turns the sign around, so a greater-than-or-equal statement becomes a less-than-or-equal solution.

The graph must show a filled circle at 5 with the line shaded to the left. Adding 6 to both sides of a negative right-hand side gives a positive boundary, so check the circle is not drawn on the negative side.

The graph must show an open circle at negative 3 with the line shaded to the left. Dividing by the positive 7 keeps the direction even though the answer is negative; a negative answer is not by itself a reason to turn the sign around.

The graph must show an open circle at negative 8 with the line shaded to the right. Multiplying both sides by negative 4 turns the sign around, so a less-than statement becomes a greater-than solution and the shading points away from the negative end.

The graph must show a filled circle at 5 with the line shaded to the left. The unknown starts on the right of the sign here, so the safest route is to read the finished statement from the letter outwards before drawing anything.
The graph must show an open circle at negative 7 with the line shaded to the right. Dividing both sides by negative 5 turns the less-than into a greater-than.
The graph must show a filled circle at negative 6 with the line shaded to the left.

Student must justify the turned-around sign with a test value taken from the graph, not merely quote the rule. A correct response tries a number in the shaded region, for example negative 10, shows it satisfies the original statement, and tries a number on the other side, for example 0, and shows it does not. Full credit needs at least one number tested in the original inequality and the conclusion drawn from it.
